title: Rapid plays: Engineering trio messaging (ML, backend, platform)
body:
Purpose: a compact set of call openings, technical proof points, and objection-handling tailored to three decision-making personas (ML engineers, backend engineers, platform teams). Use as quick riffs for SDRs, solutions engineers, and product marketing when prepping demos and proposals.

Executive one-liners (pick 1):
- ML engineers: "Serve models at production scale with GPU-aware batching and KV cache without reengineering your training stack."
- Backend engineers: "Drop in a predictable API with per-route latency SLOs and clear cost controls — no model ops heavy lifting."
- Platform teams: "Unified runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so you get one SLA and one operational model for all teams."

Micro-scripts (30–90s):
- ML engineer opener: "What takes you the most ops time today — model quantization, kernel tuning, or keeping KV caches happy? With Redwood, teams reduce manual kernel tuning by using our model profiles and runtime heuristics; you keep your model artifacts and we handle the rest."
- Backend engineer opener: "If you could replace one custom endpoint with a managed, autoscaling route that includes token-level cost telemetry, would you? We map routes to models and autoscale/downgrade to cheaper variants when latency permits."
- Platform team opener: "How many different stacks do you run for inference across product teams? Redwood gives one control plane that supports VPC/private deployments + hosted fallbacks so SREs get one set of alerts."

Key technical proof points (short bullets to cite during demo):
- Serving runtime: continuous batching with sequence-length-aware windowing; real-time KV cache eviction metrics.
- Kernel selection: per-model performance profiles that auto-select int8/quantized kernels based on latency SLOs and histogram of sequence lengths.
- Smart routing: policy-based routing (latency-first, cost-first, region-first) with automatic compatible-variant fallback.
- Observability: token-level cost attribution, per-request traces, and prompt-set regression alerts.

Persona-specific value metrics to highlight:
- ML engineers: throughput (tokens/sec per GPU), percent reduction in manual kernel tuning, time-to-serve for new model (hrs).
- Backend engineers: 95th percentile latency, cost per 1k tokens normalized to baseline, error-rate fallback counts.
- Platform teams: mean time to onboard a team (days), cross-team variance in latency (std dev), single-pane health coverage (% routes under SLO).

Anticipated objections + counters: 
- "We want to keep models on-prem only" → Can do private deployments with customer-managed control plane; we also offer an on-prem package and KMS/HSM integrations.
- "We already have infra for batching" → Most in-house batching lacks model-aware kernel selection and prefix/KV caching; we have telemetry-driven suggestions that often cut per-token cost 15–40%. Suggest a 2-week pilot on a low-risk route.
- "Cost unknown / vendor lock-in" → Transparent per-token breakdown and model variant routing reduces cost; you can pin model versions and export telemetry. For regulatory accounts we support dedicated capacity and exportable logs.

Competitive notes (concise, non-exhaustive):
- Cloud providers (big infra vendors): strong managed infra but often limited model/quantization guidance and higher variance in per-token economics. Win: unified inference-first API and lower ops for model-specialized workloads.
- Lightweight runtimes/self-hosted open source: low unit cost but high integration and staffing burden. Win: faster path to production with observable regressions and SLA options.
- Inference-specialist competitors: may match some performance; Redwood differentiators are combined routing/fallback policies, built-in cost attribution, and integrated rollouts for canaries and A/B tests.

Suggested demo flow (10–18 minutes):
1) 60s: persona-tailored opener (pick from Micro-scripts).
2) 3–5 min: show console route creation, pinning model version, and policy selection.
3) 3–4 min: live trace of a slow request, show KV cache hit/miss and fallback to cheaper variant.
4) 2–3 min: show cost telemetry (token breakdown) and a suggested Optimize recommendation for batching/quantization.
5) 2 min: rollout example (canary and auto-fallback on error spike).

PoC checklist (for SEs):
- baseline telemetry for 72h from customer route, sample prompt set (100 prompts), target SLOs for latency and availability, success criteria (<= X% cost improvement or <= Yms 95th latency).
- tickets to open: JIRA ticket for pilot (GO2M-842), infra access checklist, data retention/KMS review.

Rehearsal switches (variations):
- For skeptical backend engs, emphasise API parity and code examples (cURL/Go snippets) and show how easy rollback is.
- For platform SREs, skip model internals and deep-dive into alerts, audit logs, and network topology for private deployments.
- For ML engineers, bring a short perf table comparing their current float32 baseline vs quantized variants on sequence length buckets.

Open questions / follow-ups to scope per account:
- Which internal teams already own model versioning? (Git tags, MLflow?)
- Any regulatory + audit needs for logs retention or HSM integration?
- Typical prompt length distribution and 95th percentile sequence length for their user traffic.

Sticky language (phrases we should use consistently):
- "One runtime, three modes" (hosted / dedicated / private).
- "Predictable inference economics".
- "Model-aware serving".

Notes to self (experimental messaging to A/B test):
- Try a cost-first opener for startups: "If you cut per-token cost by 20% without changing model outputs, how many more users can you afford to serve?"
- For enterprise procurement, lead with SLA + control plane exportability and a brief diagram showing network flows for VPC/private.

Appendix: quick references to internal assets
- Pilot template: confluence:GG-serve-pilot-template (use for PoC checklist)
- Benchmarks: github:benchmarks/seqlen-profiles-2025 (use for perf table)
- Legal: shared_drives/legal/inf-run-templates (routing for contract clauses)

Document history: created 2025-11-20 by Ava Patel; edits and notes collected during SE practice sessions 2025-11-24 and 2025-12-01 (Marcus, Elena).
